history.heading: A remote discovery
paragraphs: Bouvet Island, in the South Atlantic Ocean, is often called the most remote island in the world: the nearest land, Antarctica, is about 1,700 km away. It was discovered in 1739 by the French navigator Jean-Baptiste Charles Bouvet de Lozier, who could not land and miscalculated its position, so it was not found again for decades.
Norway claimed the island after a 1927 expedition, and Britain dropped a competing claim. Bouvet Island became a Norwegian dependency in 1930.

culture.heading: Uninhabited
paragraphs: Bouvet Island has no permanent population. About 93 percent of it is covered by glaciers. Its only regular visitors are scientists and occasional expeditions; Norway maintains an automated weather station and a small research hut there.

politics.heading: Norwegian dependency
paragraphs: Bouvet Island is a dependency of Norway, administered by the Norwegian Polar Institute. It is not part of the Kingdom of Norway proper and is not covered by the Antarctic Treaty, since it lies north of 60° South. The island and its surrounding waters are a nature reserve.

economy.heading: No economic activity
paragraphs: There is no economic activity on Bouvet Island. The surrounding waters attract seals, seabirds and penguins, and fishing vessels operate in the wider region. The island has its own internet domain, .bv, which is not in use.
